source: Fleming (2001) Recombinant uncertainty in technological search, Management Science 47(1):117-132
finding: Theory: inventors search locally because of bounded rationality. Familiar components and refined combinations make an invention more useful on average and less variable. New components or combinations lower the mean but widen the spread, which yields both failures and breakthroughs. Five hypotheses: H1 familiar components raise usefulness, H2 they cut uncertainty, H3 refining a combination raises usefulness, H4 it cuts uncertainty, H5 cumulative use of one combination lowers usefulness (exhaustion).
numbers: Five hypotheses; built on March 1991 exploration and exploitation, Nelson and Winter, Kauffman, and Weitzman's combinatoric explosion.
quote: Experimentation with new components and new combinations leads to less useful inventions on average, but it also implies an increase in the variability
limits: Theory only; no causal identification. Learning, exhaustion and product life-cycle effects are not separable in the data (author says so).
agent_relevance: Gives O7 a precise rule: distance from known parts trades mean for variance. Do not expect a higher mean from far search.

source: Fleming (2001) Recombinant uncertainty in technological search, Management Science 47(1):117-132 - data and design
finding: Unit is every US patent granted May-June 1990. Usefulness is the count of later patents citing it. Components are USPTO subclasses; a combination is the set of subclasses on a patent. Histories came from before July 1990, citations from after. A negative binomial count model gives the mean, and a dispersion model gives the variance.
numbers: n = 17,264 patents. Citations mean 3.80, SD 4.88, max 110. Component familiarity mean 0.60 (max 2.28). Combination familiarity mean 0.28 (max 11.25). Cumulative combination use mean 0.62 (max 26.76).
limits: Cross-section of two randomly chosen months; one patent system; patenting differs by field; a subclass is only a proxy for a component; unpatented work is invisible.
agent_relevance: Shows how distance from the known can be computed in code from counts of past use, with no model judgement (fits G5, G8).

source: Fleming (2001) Recombinant uncertainty in technological search, Management Science 47(1):117-132 - component familiarity (H1, H2)
finding: H1 supported: familiar components raise expected citations. H2 NOT supported as stated: the effect on variance is non-monotonic. Variance falls up to the 60th percentile of familiarity, then the effect becomes less negative and turns positive at the 96th percentile. Very familiar components bring more risk, not less.
numbers: Highest vs lowest familiarity: +147% citations (coefficient 0.3958 in Model 3; e^(0.3958*2.28)=2.47). +1 SD familiarity: +11.3% expected citations. Maximum variance cut 9.6% at the 60th percentile (value 0.5992); sign flips at the 96th percentile.
limits: The first-order term alone became insignificant without controls (model not shown). Fits the view that breakthroughs come from new combinations of well-used components (Usher, Utterback) but this is not tested directly.
agent_relevance: Mix old parts in new ways: the most familiar parts give the highest-variance tail. A pure stay-close rule does not minimise variance at the extreme.

source: Fleming (2001) Recombinant uncertainty in technological search, Management Science 47(1):117-132 - combination familiarity and exhaustion (H3, H4, H5)
finding: H3 and H4 supported: refining a combination used before raises mean usefulness and lowers variance, monotonically. H5 supported: the more a combination has already been used, the less useful the next invention that uses it (exhaustion of recombinant potential).
numbers: Combination familiarity at max 11.25 vs 0: +332% citations; +1 SD: +10.3%. Variance is 2.2% lower at the mean (familiarity 0.28, mean 3.80 citations) and 64% lower at the maximum. Cumulative use at max 26.76: only 37.9% of the citations of zero prior use; +1 SD: -5.6%. Familiarity and cumulative use are highly correlated (inflates standard errors).
limits: Cumulative-use effect could also be a normal life-cycle pattern (author: models cannot reject this). Split-half checks kept signs but not always significance.
agent_relevance: Refinement helps and reuse of one recipe too often hurts: supports a cap on repeat use of one operator or analogue (G12-style budget).

source: Fleming (2001) Recombinant uncertainty in technological search, Management Science 47(1):117-132 - limits stated by the author
finding: Author lists limits: patents miss unpatented and unimportant work; firms differ in propensity to patent; subclass is a coarse proxy; no industry controls; the mean results may be a life-cycle artefact. The variance results are said to be safe from that artefact because the mean variables act as controls.
numbers: Two months of data, 17,264 patents; random split and split by month kept the signs.
limits: Financial and software patents, classified in few subclasses, may not reflect recombinant search at all.
agent_relevance: Do not over-read the mean effects; the variance claim is the sturdier one for the schema.

source: Fleming (2001) Recombinant uncertainty in technological search, Management Science 47(1):117-132 - strategy implications
finding: Advice: organisations seeking breakthroughs should try new combinations, possibly with old components, and accept more failures. Failures are partly unavoidable because search is partly blind and outcomes are very skewed. Cheap screening of nascent inventions raises the value of high-variance trials (drug screening is the example). Science can shorten search on hard landscapes.
numbers: No new numbers. Notes that portfolio averaging fails because of extreme skew.
limits: Strategy statement, not tested in the paper.
agent_relevance: Matches SCHEMA: generate widely only if S4 TEST is cheap and code-run; widen variance only with a strong filter (G8).

source: Uzzi, Mukherjee, Stringer, Jones (2013) Atypical combinations and scientific impact, Science 342:468-472
finding: Novelty is how unusual each pair of cited journals is, against a randomised citation network (z-score per pair). Two paper stats: median z (conventionality) and 10th-percentile z (tail novelty). Most papers are very conventional. Best impact comes from a highly conventional base plus a small dose of atypical pairs.
numbers: 17.9 million Web of Science papers. Only 3.54% (1980s) and 2.67% (1990s) have median z below 0; 40.8% and 40.7% have 10th-percentile z below 0. Hit = top 5% of 8-year citations. Hit rate per 100: high conventionality + high tail novelty 9.11 (about double the 5% base); conventional only 5.82; novel tail only 5.33; neither 2.05. Group shares 6.7%, 23%, 26%, 44%. P<0.00001.
quote: papers with an injection of novelty into an otherwise exceptionally familiar mass of prior work are unusually likely to have high impact
limits: Journal pairs are a coarse unit; citations proxy impact; supplement says it holds in 243 fields and for top 1% and 10% hits (supplement not opened).
agent_relevance: Direct support for a mixed design: mostly familiar material with a few distant parts. Gives a test the agent can copy: a numeric tail-novelty share.

source: Uzzi et al. (2013) - peak conventionality and teams
finding: Peak impact is at the 85th to 95th percentile of median conventionality, an extremely high level, whatever the novelty or team size. Past that peak the relation reverses. Tail novelty adds impact at every conventionality level. Teams add tail novelty without losing conventionality.
numbers: Tail novelty share: 36.1% solo, 39.8% pairs, 49.7% for 3 or more authors (+37.7% over solo). Median conventionality does not differ by team size (K-S P 0.768, 0.417, 0.164).
limits: Observational; team effects confounded with field and resources.
agent_relevance: Suggests the best share of distant parts is small, not 50-50.

source: Wang, Veugelers, Stephan (2017) Bias against novelty in science, Research Policy 46:1416-1436 (NBER w22180 version read)
finding: Novelty = first-ever pairs of cited journals, weighted by how hard the pair is to make. Highly novel papers are cited more on average, have wider spread, are more often top-1% hits in the long run, but are slow to be recognised and appear in lower impact-factor journals. Fleming's mean-variance pattern is replicated for papers, with the mean gain only for highly novel work.
numbers: All 2001 WoS articles: 773,311 total, 674,546 with 2+ WoS references; 89% make no new journal pair. Highly novel = top 1% novelty in field. Mean citations +12.04% (moderately novel +2.78%); dispersion +14.90% (highly novel only). Odds of top-1% hit +39.82% (highly), +11.22% (moderately). Highly novel papers do worse in a window under 3 years and better from year 4; moderately novel need 9+ years. Journal impact factor -18.11% and -10.55%.
quote: novel research is also more risky, reflected by a higher variance in its citation performance
limits: One journal-pair proxy; one publication year; moderately novel papers do worse in their home field; Bornmann validation of the same type of score found weak agreement for score W (see a18).
agent_relevance: Early evaluation under-rates novel ideas: an agent that judges ideas on a short window will reject them (G8).

source: Youn, Bettencourt, Strumsky, Lobo (2015) Invention as a combinatorial process: evidence from US patents, J. R. Soc. Interface 12
finding: US patents 1790-2010 treated as sets of technology codes. 77% of patents combine 2 or more codes; single-code patents fell from nearly half in the 19th century to about 12%. New codes enter slowly but new combinations of codes keep appearing at a steady rate: C = 0.6 P.
numbers: Distinct combinations C grow linearly with patents P, slope about 0.6: about 60% of new patents make a never-seen combination, about 40% reuse one. Random choice would repeat a combination with probability about 1e-4 at T = 10,000 codes. Share of narrow (same class) multi-code patents about 44% overall; about 50% before 1930, about 30% after WWII, about 50% now.
quote: The search strategy implicit in the process of invention seems to be poised halfway between exploration and exploitation
limits: Counts new combinations, not their quality; relies on examiner classification codes.
agent_relevance: Gives a base rate: about 60/40 new versus reused recipe in real invention. A usable default for how often O7 tries a new pairing.

source: Youn et al. (2015) - reuse is uneven
finding: Use of single codes and of combinations is highly uneven and far from random. A rich-get-richer effect tied to age is hardly seen: being older does not by itself make a code more used.
numbers: Heavy-tailed frequency of use, Yule-Simon-like, with no clear link to vintage.
limits: Descriptive; no performance outcome.
agent_relevance: Reuse concentrates on a few components. An analogue library may do the same, which is the exhaustion risk in H5.

source: Foster, Rzhetsky, Evans (2015) Tradition and innovation in scientists' research strategies, American Sociological Review 80(5)
finding: Biomedical chemistry network built from MEDLINE. Five strategies: jump (new chemical), new consolidation, new bridge, repeat consolidation, repeat bridge. Rarer strategies bring more citations but more spread; prize winners and highly cited work use more jumps and consolidations.
numbers: 6,455,756 abstracts (1934-2008); network 181,078 chemicals and 84,709,977 links by 2008; analysis 1983-2008. Repeat 85.8% vs new or jump 14.2%; new bridge or consolidation 12.4% vs jump 1.8%. Mean citations 8.38 repeat, 11.00 new, 12.90 jump. Surprisal explains 29.2% of variation in mean citations and 28.6% in the SD. Prize study: 137 prizes, 7,594 awardees, 241,176 articles.
limits: Only published work is seen, so failed risky projects are invisible; mean citations used as utility; the strategy mix stayed stable while the space grew 22x to 188x.
agent_relevance: Second source for rare means higher mean and higher SD; the stable mix suggests a norm of few jumps on a base of tradition.

source: Verhoeven, Bakker, Veugelers (2016) Measuring technological novelty with patent-based indicators, Research Policy 45:707-723 (working paper MSI_1509 read)
finding: Extends Fleming's method to all major patent offices with three novelty indicators: new pairs of IPC classes (recombination), new pairs of cited technology classes, new scientific fields cited. Novel patents have higher variance and more outliers, but only patents novel on all three dimensions have higher mean impact; other novel patents have a lower mean.
numbers: Utility filings 1980-2011 (PATSTAT). About 260,000 families (about 7% of those that make combinations) make a new combination; 7% of those make over 5 new ones. Outliers: 3.3% at 2 SD, 0.5% at 5 SD. Patents with new scientific origins have 52% higher odds of a 5 SD outlier; novel on all three dimensions 126% higher odds. Only 1.8% of the R&D-award sample is novel in scientific origin.
limits: 7-year citation window, families to 2003. Most patents score on a single novelty indicator.
agent_relevance: Confirms the variance and outlier effect with new data. Adds that novelty from several independent sources together is what lifts the mean.

source: Lee, Walsh, Wang (2015) Creativity in scientific teams: unpacking novelty and impact, Research Policy 44 (accepted manuscript read)
finding: Adapts Uzzi's journal-pair measure to an ex ante novelty score and tests team features. Team size has an inverted-U relation with novelty but a rising relation with high impact. Knowledge variety (fields, tasks) drives novelty; team size, not variety, drives impact once novelty is controlled.
numbers: Survey: 8,864 papers sampled, 3,742 scientists replied (42%), 2,327 full replies (26%). Novelty turns down after about +1 SD team size (about 7 authors) while impact keeps rising. Novelty has a positive and significant effect on impact (probit).
limits: 26% full response rate; probit; limited field mix.
agent_relevance: Novelty and impact have different drivers. An agent should separate making a distant combination from making it get used.

source: Ke, Teng, Min (2021, v2 2024) Relying on recent and temporally dispersed science predicts breakthrough inventions (arXiv 2107.09176)
finding: Patents that cite scientific papers get more citations and are more likely to be breakthroughs. Citing more recent papers raises impact. The gain is offset if the cited papers' ages have low variance. Holds across technology fields.
numbers: Abstract and introduction read; effect sizes not extracted.
limits: Only abstract-level results extracted.
agent_relevance: Age mix of sources, not only distance, is a lever for O7: recent plus spread beats uniform.

source: Li, Lin, Wu (2024) Can recombination growth lead to scientific breakthroughs? (preprint, file read)
finding: Counter-evidence. Across 19 million papers over a century, reference atypicality correlates negatively with disruption in every field, period and team size. Comparing early and later versions of 2,461 papers, adding atypical references lowers disruption of the same paper. Breakthroughs are framed as replacing old ideas, not only joining them.
numbers: 20 breakthrough papers nominated by 20 scientists have mean D 0.21 (top 2%); papers nominated as developing -0.011 (bottom 13%); AUC 0.83. One panel reports slope -0.0009 (P<0.05).
limits: Disruption is a different outcome from usefulness or hit rate; the D index is contested; nominations come from only 20 scientists. No URL recorded; title searched on arXiv returned no match.
agent_relevance: Novel mix is not the same as a replacing idea. A distant analogue should be tested for whether it replaces the incumbent approach.

source: Li, Lin, Wu (2025) Can recombination displace dominant scientific ideas? (arXiv 2506.15959)
finding: Larger replication of the negative atypicality-disruption link. Atypicality marks cross-topic extension; disruption marks replacement of a dominant idea within its topic. An LLM (Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct, zero shot) labels the breakthrough type of 50,147 disruptive and highly cited papers.
numbers: 40,935,251 articles 1965-2020 in the results (abstract says 41 million, 1965-2024). Top 5% atypical: A > 22.9; top 5% displacing: D > 0.04.
limits: Preprint; LLM labels not validated in the part read.
agent_relevance: An early use of an LLM as a classifier inside this literature.

source: Bornmann et al. (2019/2020) Do we measure novelty when we analyze unusual combinations of cited references? J. Informetrics (arXiv 1910.03233)
finding: Validity test of the Uzzi-style score U and the Wang-style score W against F1000Prime faculty tags. Score U agrees with expert novelty tags; score W mostly does not.
numbers: One SD up on score U: +7.47% expected new-finding tags. Score W shows weak or no agreement with the tags.
limits: Biomedical papers only; F1000Prime tags are a noisy criterion.
agent_relevance: A distance score must be checked against a human or run-based criterion before it steers the agent (G3, G8).

source: Tria, Loreto, Servedio, Strogatz (2014) The dynamics of correlated novelties, Scientific Reports 4:5890
finding: Formal model: a Polya urn that adds new possible things each time a novelty occurs (expanding the adjacent possible). It predicts Heaps' law for the rate of novelties and Zipf's law for use, plus a signature that one novelty opens others. Tested on four data sets.
numbers: Data: Wikipedia edits, tags, words in texts, new songs listened to online.
limits: Models the rate of novelty, not quality or usefulness (abstract and intro read).
agent_relevance: A cheap code-level model of how fast the search space grows after each new combination.

source: Weitzman (1998) Recombinant growth, Quarterly Journal of Economics 113(2):331-360
finding: Growth model where new ideas come from recombining old ones, like cross-pollinating plant varieties. The number of possible subsets grows as 2^M, so the supply of seed ideas explodes. The binding limit becomes the ability to turn seed ideas into usable form, not the supply of ideas.
numbers: Pairs C(M,2); full power set C(M)=2^M; a theorem gives long-run growth as a function of savings in research and in other output.
quote: the ultimate limits to growth may lie not so much in our ability to generate new ideas, so much as in our ability to process an abundance of potentially new seed ideas into usable form
limits: Theory only; no data; assumes each pair can be tried at a cost.
agent_relevance: Candidate generation is cheap and unbounded; testing and development is the scarce step. Fits G8 and G5: put budget into the test, not more ideas.

source: Pichler, Lafond, Farmer (2020) Technological interdependencies predict innovation dynamics (arXiv 2003.00580)
finding: Network model: a technology domain's innovation rate depends on the rates of the domains it relies on. Fitted on US patents 1836-2017.
numbers: Out-of-sample forecasts: 28% better than time-series models when neighbours' future rates are known, 20% better when not.
limits: Predicts patenting rates, not quality; abstract-level read.
agent_relevance: Support for choosing analogue sources that are themselves active and well supplied.

source: Fleming and Sorenson (2001) Technology as a complex adaptive system: evidence from patent data, Research Policy 30(7):1019-1039
finding: Not opened (paywalled). Known only from search listings: treats invention as search on a fitness landscape where components interact; more interdependence makes search harder.
numbers: Not available this session.
limits: Full text unread; do not cite numbers.
agent_relevance: Link to the NK landscape view of O7: more interacting parts means harder recombination.

source: Fleming and Sorenson (2004) Science as a map in technological search, Strategic Management Journal 25:909-928
finding: Abstract only (OpenAlex): science helps inventors by pointing to useful combinations, removing fruitless paths and keeping them going after negative feedback. It helps most when the components are highly coupled.
numbers: Not extracted.
limits: Full text unread.
agent_relevance: A map (theory or checks) helps most where parts interact strongly: use theory-guided search for coupled sub-problems.

source: Katila and Ahuja (2002) Something old, something new, Academy of Management Journal 45(6)
finding: Abstract only: in global robotics, firms' search varies on two dimensions, search depth (how often existing knowledge is reused) and search scope (how widely new knowledge is explored), not on one local-to-distant line.
numbers: Abstract only; PDF text could not be extracted.
limits: Full text unread; effect sizes not verified.
agent_relevance: Treat how much to reuse and how far to look as two separate dials in O7.

source: Kaplan and Vakili (2015) The double-edged sword of recombination in breakthrough innovation, Strategic Management Journal 36(10):1435-1457
finding: From summaries: topic modelling shows patents that start new topics come more from local search, while the most useful (highly cited) patents come from broader recombination. Novelty and usefulness have different roots.
numbers: 2,826 nanotechnology patents (search summary).
limits: Full text unread; one technology field.
agent_relevance: Challenges a single distance dial: novel ideas may come from near search and valuable ones from far search.

source: Singh and Fleming (2010) Lone inventors as sources of breakthroughs, Management Science 56(1):41-56
finding: Abstract (OpenAlex): collaboration trims the bad tail and lifts the good tail at once, so it is not just higher variance. Lone inventors make fewer breakthroughs and more very poor outcomes. Quantile regressions show more than a mean shift.
numbers: Over half a million patented inventions.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: A second reader (selection) cuts the bad tail while diversity lifts the good tail: both needed for O7.

source: Levinthal (1997) Adaptation on rugged landscapes, Management Science 43(7):934-950
finding: Abstract only: when attributes interact, the fitness landscape has many peaks, the starting point decides which peak is found, and tightly coupled organisations fail more in changing environments.
numbers: Not extracted.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Formal base (Kauffman NK) for the claim that interacting parts make combination search hard.

source: Arthur and Polak (2006) The evolution of technology within a simple computer model, Complexity 11(5):23-31
finding: From secondary summaries: starting from NAND gates, random combination plus stepping-stone rewards evolved circuits such as an 8-bit adder; complex designs appear only after simpler intermediate ones exist.
numbers: Combines 2 to 12 existing parts per step (secondary source).
limits: Not opened; secondary summary only.
agent_relevance: Recombination works when verified simpler parts are kept as building blocks: keep verified sub-results.

source: Fleming (2007) Breakthroughs and the long tail of innovation, MIT Sloan Management Review 49(1)
finding: Summary only: invention outcomes are very skewed; most are useless, a few are breakthroughs; judge a process by shots on goal, average score and maximum score.
numbers: None extracted.
limits: Search summary only.
agent_relevance: Score a search design on its best result as well as its mean.
